source.title_on_document: Think First, ChatGPT Later: Guiding Human–AI Collaboration for Learning Gains in Independent Human Creativity

supplement.where: The paper refers to no supplementary material or online appendix. Appendices A to E (task instructions, AUT flexibility categories, sample responses) are inside this PDF (pp. 33-41). Data and analysis code are on OSF: https://osf.io/t7an8/overview?view_only=fc490583cdc8458e8b895b29e4df2345 (p. 41, Data Availability).
supplement.holds: The paper refers no creativity-contrast statistics to an external supplement. Arm means, SDs, p-values, and Cohen's d for every pairwise creativity contrast are printed in the text (pp. 20 and 22); analyzed arm ns are on p. 8 and in Table 4 (p. 20). Fig. 2 (p. 21) shows standard-error bars, but separate numerical standard errors or confidence intervals for the pairwise creativity effects are not printed. The authors link data and analysis code on OSF (p. 41, Data Availability); the posted files were not inspected in this final review.

paper_design_summary: In a lab experiment at a public university in Singapore, students were randomly assigned to improve a stuffed bunny alone, with free ChatGPT-4 use, or with a guided 'think first, ChatGPT later' procedure (p. 8, Design; pp. 13-14, Procedure). Of 197 students who took part, 196 were analyzed after one exclusion: human-only analyzed n = 64, general-AI analyzed n = 67, and regulated-AI analyzed n = 65; the guided arm split the 12-minute task into 3 min generating own ideas, 6 min with ChatGPT and sample prompts, and 3 min independent refinement (p. 8; p. 14). All participants then solved a 12-minute product invention task (a foreign-language vocabulary game) without ChatGPT in the same session, and two expert raters blind to condition scored each participant's single solution on each task for originality, usefulness, and elaboration on 1 to 7 scales (pp. 14-16).

studies.label: Lab experiment: product improvement task (with or without ChatGPT), then unassisted product invention task

assignment.what_was_assigned: Learning group for the product improvement task: human-only (no ChatGPT), general-AI (free ChatGPT-4 use), or regulated-AI (guided 'think first, ChatGPT later' use of ChatGPT-4 with seven sample prompts)
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three learning groups: human-only (control condition; n = 64), general-AI (n = 67), or regulated-AI (n = 65).
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration is mentioned anywhere in the document (full-text search); the OSF link is for data and code (p. 41). The paper calls the creativity outcomes 'primary outcomes' of the 'main confirmatory analyses' (p. 18, Results) without citing a registration.

arms.name: human-only
arms.description: Control condition. Solved the 12-minute product improvement task independently, with no other tabs or windows open; then solved the product invention task independently.

arms.name: general-AI
arms.description: Freely used ChatGPT-4 in a split-screen window during the 12-minute product improvement task, in any way they liked, and were told to give clear, detailed prompts; then solved the product invention task without ChatGPT.

arms.name: regulated-AI
arms.description: 'Think first, ChatGPT later': Phase 1 (3 min) generated own initial ideas alone; Phase 2 (6 min) worked with ChatGPT-4 as a brainstorming and feedback partner, with seven sample prompts shown (own prompts allowed); Phase 3 (3 min) independently refined and submitted the best idea; then solved the product invention task without ChatGPT or the sample prompts.

participants.exclusions: 197 students took part; one participant who failed to adhere to the experimental instructions was excluded from analyses, leaving 196 analyzed (p. 8, Participants). The arm counts printed with the assignment statement (64, 67, 65) sum to the 196 analyzed, so they are analyzed counts, also shown in Table 4 (p. 20). The paper does not say which arm the excluded participant was in and gives no count at assignment. An a priori power analysis targeted at least 53 participants per condition (d = 0.55, 80% power, two-tailed, alpha = .05; p. 8, Participants).
participants.who: University students aged 18 to 29 (M = 21.62, SD = 2.09; 125 female, 67 male, 5 undisclosed, of 197) from diverse majors and stages of college at a large public university in Singapore; course credit or monetary reimbursement
participants.quote: Outcomes reported below are based on data from 196 participants; one participant who failed to adhere to the experimental instructions was excluded from analyses.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4 (GPT-4 version of ChatGPT via the web interface, ChatGPT Plus subscription; default parameters, memory/model training switched off)
ai_tool.how_used: General-AI arm: free use of ChatGPT-4 in a split-screen window for the whole 12-minute product improvement task. Regulated-AI arm: 3 min generating own ideas without AI, then 6 min using ChatGPT-4 to improve, develop, and evaluate those ideas, guided by seven sample prompts (Table 1, p. 10) and told to treat it as a brainstorming and feedback partner rather than a provider of final answers, then 3 min independently refining and submitting the best idea. Neither arm had ChatGPT during the product invention task (pp. 13-14; p. 42, Reproducibility Note).

task.description: Intervention task: propose one best creative (original and useful) idea to improve an ordinary 30 cm stuffed bunny to make it more fun to play with and achieve higher sales (Appendix A, pp. 33-35). Post-intervention task: independently invent one new game that helps adults and university students learn basic foreign-language vocabulary, developed into a full game design (Appendix B, p. 35). A 2-minute Alternate Uses Task (car tire) served as a pre-treatment baseline.
task.duration: 12 min per creative task; whole session approximately 30 min (p. 13)

outcomes.name: Originality of solution on the product improvement task (intervention; ChatGPT available to the two AI arms)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two trained, experienced experts, blind to condition, rated each participant's single solution on a 1-7 originality scale following the Consensual Assessment Technique (responses viewed in a randomized order and rated relative to the pool); consistency ICC = .958, 95% CI [.945, .969]; the mean of the two ratings was analyzed (pp. 15-16). 3 (group) x 2 (task) mixed ANOVA, interaction F(2, 193) = 13.80, p < .001, partial eta squared = 0.13, then Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons (p. 20). AI availability: the general-AI arm had ChatGPT-4 for all 12 minutes; the regulated-AI arm used ChatGPT-4 in Phase 2 (6 min) and wrote the scored idea in a 3-minute Phase 3 that the paper calls independent (p. 14). The paper does not say whether the ChatGPT window was closed in Phase 3.

eligibility.reason: The paper explicitly reports random assignment of participants to human-only, general-AI, or regulated-AI for a creative product improvement task (p. 8, Design). The general-AI arm freely used ChatGPT-4 and human-only worked without it (pp. 13-14, Procedure; p. 42, Reproducibility Note). There were 196 people analyzed after one exclusion, with analyzed arm counts of 64/67/65 (p. 8, Participants and Design; Table 4, p. 20). Two trained experts blind to condition scored the participants' submitted solutions for originality, usefulness, and elaboration, and their mean ratings were analyzed (pp. 15-16, Scoring Procedure). A subsequent creative task was completed without ChatGPT in the same session (pp. 13-14). All three criteria are met; the remaining uncertainties about the guided arm's final phase, allocation details, and possible thesis overlap do not change eligibility, which is independently supported by general-AI versus human-only.

one_line_finding: With ChatGPT available, free use raised expert-rated originality over no AI (4.08 vs 3.06, d = 0.79, p < .001) while guided 'think first, ChatGPT later' use did not (3.30, d = 0.18, p = .90); on the next task, done without AI in the same session, free users matched the no-AI group (2.69 vs 2.63, d = 0.04) and the guided group scored higher than both (3.42; d = 0.52 vs no AI, d = 0.48 vs free use) (p. 20, Fig. 2A on p. 21).
open_questions: S1-O1 to S1-O3, regulated-AI arm: the scored idea was written in a 3-minute Phase 3 that the paper calls independent, right after a 6-minute ChatGPT phase, and the paper does not say whether the ChatGPT window stayed open in Phase 3 (p. 14; Appendix A, p. 35). The form codes ai_available_when_produced = yes because the paper says both AI groups completed this task with ChatGPT assistance (p. 9). Review 1 may want to flag the regulated-AI with_ai contrasts.
Per-arm randomized counts are not stated: the arm ns printed with the assignment statement (64/67/65) sum to the 196 analyzed, and the arm of the one excluded participant is not given (p. 8).

The search record lists an NUS bachelor's thesis (Qiu 2025, 'Think First, ChatGPT Later: Collaborative AI Use Sustains Creativity in Problem-Solving Even After Tool Removal') as an earlier version. This article does not mention it, so whether the thesis reports the same participants is not stated in the document. The funding note names a Yale-NUS College Capstone Research grant to Qiu (p. 41).

The regulated-AI arm differs from the general-AI arm in time structure (3 min own ideas, 6 min ChatGPT, 3 min writing), instructions, and sample prompts, so the regulated vs general contrast bundles the AI configuration with less time on ChatGPT and less time to write (p. 14; p. 29). Regulated-AI vs human-only also bundles AI access with guidance: the paper identifies a matched 'regulated-human' condition as a future comparison, not a condition in this experiment (p. 32, Limitations and Future Directions). This is an established limitation of attribution, not an unresolved eligibility criterion.
notes: Single lab experiment: groups of up to five per session, each participant seated alone at a computer, about 30 min in total (pp. 12-13). Assignment is described at the participant level; the paper does not say whether conditions varied within a session. The Alternate Uses Task (fluency, flexibility) is a pre-treatment baseline, not an outcome (no group differences: fluency F(2, 193) = 0.30, p = .74; flexibility F(2, 193) = 0.32, p = .73; p. 19, Table 3). Not coded because they are self-reports: self-assessed originality and usefulness, interest, motivation, mental effort, exhaustion, task difficulty, creative self-efficacy, metacognition (MCPS), perceived collaboration with ChatGPT, reliance on ChatGPT, and usefulness of ChatGPT (Table 3, p. 19; pp. 27-28). Not coded because they describe process, not scored output: prompt-type coding of ChatGPT transcripts (Table 5, p. 23), correlations of prompt types with later creativity (Table 6, p. 25), and the mediation analysis (Fig. 3, p. 26), whose indirect effects are recorded in the measure_detail of S1-O4 and S1-O5. Within-group changes across the two tasks (for example, general-AI originality fell, p < .001, d = -1.05; regulated-AI usefulness rose, p < .001, d = 0.63; pp. 20-22) compare different tasks, not arms, and are not coded as contrasts. Pairwise p-values are Bonferroni-corrected after 3 x 2 mixed ANOVAs; the analysis is at the participant level (one solution per participant per task, mean of two expert ratings; 196 scripts scored, p. 15). Fig. 2 error bars are standard errors (p. 21). Sign check: every printed d has the sign of treatment minus control as the contrasts are coded here (for example, d = -0.62 where regulated-AI's mean of 3.30 is below general-AI's 4.08), although the paper prints the regulated vs general values for originality and usefulness on the first task in sentences that name general-AI first. Under codebook section 8, the primary records are originality, general-AI vs human-only: S1-O1 for with_ai and S1-O4 for after_ai. No diversity (across_people) outcome is reported. No preregistration is mentioned. Final review (2026-10-08): read the full markdown conversion, including Appendices A-E and references, and checked the recorded numerical findings and eligibility evidence against the PDF. The publication date was verified in the embedded image on p. 1. The assignment, outcome, and people challenge files each contained an empty problems array, so final.challenge_resolution is empty and all three challenge-resolution counts are zero. No numerical result was changed. Analyzed counts are explicitly labeled in the design summary and exclusion description; remaining source gaps and the confirmed treatment-bundling limitation are assessed in final.open_items. Both reconciliation differences remain resolved, and the reconciliation object is preserved unchanged.

differences.a: mixed (A's open question: the general-AI arm had ChatGPT open while writing, and the regulated-AI arm wrote its final idea in Phase 3 without ChatGPT)

differences.resolved: yes. The paper says both AI groups completed the product improvement task with ChatGPT assistance (p. 9) and had a ChatGPT-4 window open during the intervention (p. 13). The general-AI arm, which gives the primary with_ai record, had ChatGPT for all 12 minutes. The regulated-AI arm wrote its scored idea in a 3-minute Phase 3 that the paper calls independent, 'based on your initial ideas and interaction with ChatGPT' (p. 35); the paper does not say the ChatGPT window was closed then, so A's reading that this arm had no ChatGPT in Phase 3 is not stated. The Phase 3 detail is kept in measure_detail and open_questions.

open_items.item: Regulated-AI access to ChatGPT during Phase 3 remains unstated: the paper calls refinement independent, but describes the product improvement task as AI-assisted (pp. 9, 13-14; Appendix A, p. 35). Authors could confirm whether ChatGPT was closed or further use prohibited during this phase. This affects the guided arm's with_ai/after_ai classification, not any core criterion: general-AI versus human-only independently qualifies.

Counts at randomization and the excluded participant's arm are not reported (p. 8, Participants and Design). Authors' allocation and exclusion records would settle them. Randomized counts remain null; the confirmed 196 people analyzed, with analyzed arm counts 64/67/65, already meet the sample-size criterion (p. 8; Table 4, p. 20).

Possible participant overlap with the Qiu 2025 NUS thesis is an unverified search-record lead; the journal article does not identify the thesis, and the capstone funding statement alone cannot establish shared participants (p. 41). Author confirmation comparing the thesis and journal samples would settle deduplication. This does not alter any of the journal study's eligibility criteria.

Bundling of the regulated-AI protocol with time limits, guidance, and sample prompts is established in the PDF (p. 14; p. 29); the absence of a matched regulated-human arm is acknowledged on p. 32. Nothing further is needed for screening: retain regulated-AI versus general-AI as ai_design and versus human-only as ai_vs_bau, while treating them as effects of the combined intervention. Isolating the guidance contribution would require a new comparison; general-AI versus human-only already supports eligibility.

The randomization method and whether sessions mixed conditions are unstated. Participants were described as randomly assigned, but attended lab sessions of up to five (p. 8; pp. 12-13). Authors could clarify individual versus session allocation and any clustering needed for standard errors. This does not negate the reported random assignment or the confirmed number of people analyzed, so it does not change the present eligibility decision.
